claims.claim: Gen 8:20 records the first altar in the Bible: Noah builds an altar and offers ʿōlâ of clean animals and birds only.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 8:20 read directly (BibleGateway); BDB mizbēaḥ sense 1: "J E narrate that altars were built by Noah after leaving the ark Gen 8:20"; BDB ʿōlâ lists Gen 8:20 first for the phrase heʿĕlâ ʿōlâ. Interlinear Gen 8 read directly.

claims.claim: ʿōlâ (H5930) is the whole burnt offering, entirely consumed — "that which goes up" — matching the verb way·ya·ʿal (Hiphil of ʿālāh, "cause to go up") in the same verse.
claims.evidence: BDB ʿōlâ I, read directly: "whole burnt-offering (beast or fowl) is entirely consumed and goes up in the flame of the altar to God".

claims.claim: rêaḥ hannîḥôaḥ (8:21) is the fixed idiom "soothing/restful aroma", and Gen 8:21 is its first occurrence in the Bible; the literal force is "an aroma that brings rest/quieting".
claims.evidence: BDB nîḥôaḥ (H5207), read directly: "only in phrase rêaḥ nîḥôaḥ = soothing, tranquillizing odour of sacrifices acceptable to YHWH, Gen 8:21 (J)…". BDB rêaḥ (H7381) cites 8:21 as a construct occurrence.

claims.claim: The divine resolve in 8:21 is spoken "in his heart" (ʾel-lib·bōw) — a soliloquy, not addressed to Noah.
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 8 read directly: way·yō·mer Yah·weh ʾel-lib·bōw.

claims.claim: 8:21 states the resolve *despite* the unchanged human diagnosis: lō-ʾōsîp̄ ("I will not continue/add") twice, each with ʿō·wḏ, with kî introducing the yeṣer clause. The flood changed God's response, not human nature.
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 8 read directly; Gen 6:5 interlinear read directly (yê·ṣer maḥ·šə·ḇōṯ lib·bōw — the same diagnosis).

claims.claim: yeṣer (H3336) in 8:21 is "what is framed in the mind" — the heart's inclination or intent — the same word as Gen 6:5.
claims.evidence: BDB yeṣer senses 1–3 + sense 4 opening ("of what is framed in the mind"), read directly; Gen 6:5 interlinear confirms the parallel use. Caveat: the full BDB sense-4 wording is partially verified only (page truncates mid-sentence — see §14); the claim itself rests on the verified opening + the interlinear parallel.

claims.claim: 8:22 ordains four paired opposites (seedtime/harvest, cold/heat, summer/winter, day/night) that "shall not cease" (lō yiš·bō·ṯū, from šāḇaṯ) — an ordinance covering the whole order of nature.
claims.evidence: KJV + interlinear Gen 8 read directly.

claims.claim: The 9:1 blessing triad pĕrû ûrĕbû ûmilʾû is the exact Gen 1:28 triad.
claims.evidence: BDB pārâ (H6509) cites "pĕrû ûrĕbû ûmilʾû… Gen 1:22, 28; Gen 9:1"; BDB rābâ (H7235) likewise. Interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: In 9:2 dominion is reframed as fear (mōrāʾ) and dread (ḥat) falling on the animals; the fourfold list matches Gen 1:26, 28; "into your hand they are given" is Nifal perfect — a completed grant.
claims.evidence: BDB mōrāʾ sense 1 cites Gen 9:2 with ḥat as its parallel; BDB ḥat sense I is built on Gen 9:2. Interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: The 9:3 meat permission is explicitly patterned on Gen 1:29–30: the same verb nā·ṯat·tî and the same phrase lə·ʾāḵ·lāh ("for food"), with the comparison kə·ye·req ʿê·śeḇ ("as the green plant").
claims.evidence: Gen 1:29–30 interlinear read directly: 1:29 nā·ṯat·tî… kāl-ʿê·śeḇ… lə·ʾāḵ·lāh; 1:30 kāl-ye·req ʿê·śeḇ lə·ʾāḵ·lāh to every ne·p̄eš ḥay·yāh. Difference recorded: in Gen 1 the plant is given to the animals; in Gen 9 meat is given to humans on that pattern.

claims.claim: Gen 9:4 states the blood = life equation explicitly: "flesh with its life, [namely] its blood" (bə·nap̄·šōw ḏā·mōw).
claims.evidence: BDB dām sense 1: "blood of man or animal, = the life (nepeš) Gen 9:4 (P)"; BDB nephesh sense 3a: "a living being whose life resides in the blood… in P Gen 9:4, 5". Both read directly.

claims.claim: In 9:5 ʾeḏ·rōš ("I will require") occurs three times — from beast, from man, from "each man's brother" — and BDB records the phrase "require blood at the hand of" (dāraš dāmô mî·yaḏ) with Gen 9:5 as its citation.
claims.evidence: BDB dām sense 1k, read directly. Interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: Gen 9:6 is a perfect mirror — Qal participle šō·p̄êḵ ("whoever sheds") → Nifal imperfect yiš·šā·p̄êḵ ("shall be shed"), same root šāp̄ak, same object dām — and its rationale is creation theology: bə·ṣe·lem ʾĕ·lō·hîm.
claims.evidence: BDB šāp̄ak Qal 1b ("shed blood… Gen 9:6 (P)") and Nifal ("be shed, of blood Gen 9:6 (P)"), read directly. BDB ṣelem sense 2 cites "Gen 1:26…, Gen 1:27; Gen 9:6… (all P)".

claims.claim: The preposition in bāʾāḏām (9:6) is disputed: agent/instrument "by (means of) man" (KJV, traditional) vs. *bĕth pretii* "for [the] man" (blood shed *for* the victim, agent = God via 9:5). *No textual variant exists*; the dispute is grammatical/interpretive.
claims.evidence: Mastnjak (Church Life Journal, read directly) argues *pretii*; Finlay (reply, read directly) argues the major lexicons/grammars (GKC, BDB, BHRG, IBHS, HSTE, DCH) prefer agent/instrument, and Joüon–Muraoka p. 454 — Mastnjak's own citation — explicitly argues the traditional reading. NETS adopts the *pretii* reading ("in return for this blood shall it be shed"). Neither source cites a variant Hebrew reading.

claims.claim: The 9:7 blessing repeats 9:1 with "you" fronted (wə·ʾat·tem, emphatic) and šir·ṣū ("swarm, teem") added — the verb of Gen 1:20–21 and Gen 8:17 — so the blood law (9:4–6) sits framed inside the blessing.
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 9 and Gen 8 (8:17: wə·šā·rə·ṣū … ū·p̄ā·rū wə·rā·ḇū) read directly.

claims.claim: The covenant verb qûm (Hiphil, "establish/ratify") shifts form across the section — 9:9 mê·qîm (participle, "am establishing") → 9:11 wa·hă·qi·mō·ṯî → 9:17 hă·qi·mō·ṯî (perfects, "I have established") — and the 9:11 form is *identical* to Gen 6:18: the 9:9–17 covenant fulfils the 6:18 promise.
claims.evidence: BDB qûm Hiphil 6d, read in full (re-fetched): "*establish* (make, ratify) covenant, of YHWH… Gen 6:18; Gen 9:9, 11; Gen 17:19, 21; Exod 6:4 (all P)… with bên…bên Gen 9:17". Gen 6:18 interlinear read directly (wa·hă·qi·mō·ṯî ʾeṯ-bə·rî·ṯî ʾit·tāḵ).

claims.claim: The covenant's parties widen in four steps: Noah + seed (9:9) → every living creature, kāl-ne·p̄eš ha·ḥay·yāh (9:10) → "the earth" (9:13) → "all flesh" (9:15–17). The 9:10 phrase is the same as Gen 1:30's recipients of the green plant.
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 9 read directly; BDB nephesh sense 2: "nepeš ḥayyâ always of animals Gen 1:20, 24, 30; Gen 9:12, 15, 16 (all P)… Gen 9:10 (both P)".

claims.claim: Gen 9:11 is a double negative (no more cutting off of "all flesh", no more flood to destroy the earth), with ʿō·wḏ ("again") twice; kāraṯ ("cut off") is the verb of covenant-cutting used ironically — the covenant guarantees no more cutting off.
claims.evidence: KJV + interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: ʾôṯ (H226) in 9:12–13, 17 is the covenant-sign (BDB sense 6, citing Gen 9:12, 13, 17 alongside circumcision Gen 17:11 and the sabbath Exod 31:13, 17); qešet (H7198) is the ordinary word for a war/hunting bow, with sense 2 "rainbow" at Gen 9:13, 14, 16.
claims.evidence: BDB ʾôṯ sense 6 and BDB qešet sense 2, read directly.

claims.claim: In 9:12–13 the sign's giving is present (nō·ṯên, participle, "I am giving") while the bow is already set (nā·ṯat·tî, perfect, "I have set"); the covenant's second party widens one final step to "between me and the earth".
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: In 9:15–16 God is the subject of "remembering" the covenant (wə·zā·ḵar·tî; liz·kōr, infinitive of purpose — God looks upon the bow *in order to* remember); the same verb frames the flood story at 8:1 ("God remembered Noah").
claims.evidence: BDB zākar II.3a, read directly: "*remember* his own covenant (with them), accusative, Gen 9:15, 16; Exod 2:24…" — Gen 9:15, 16 listed first. Interlinear Gen 8 (8:1) read directly.

claims.claim: Gen 9:16 names the covenant bə·rîṯ ʿô·w·lām, "the everlasting covenant" (BDB cites Gen 9:16); the divine name in that clause is ʾĕ·lō·hîm, not YHWH.
claims.evidence: BDB bĕrît, read directly ("bərîṯ ʿôlām" cites Gen 9:16). Interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: Gen 9:17 closes the section by repeating 9:12's formula with the plain perfect hă·qi·mō·ṯî ("I have established") and the widest party formula, addressed to Noah alone.
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: The kol-bāśār ("all flesh") thread runs through Gen 6–9: the judged category (6:12 corrupt; 6:13 its end; 6:17 to be destroyed; 7:21 died) becomes the covenanted category (9:11 not cut off; 9:15–17 covenant with all flesh).
claims.evidence: Every occurrence verified in the BibleHub interlinear for Gen 6, 7, 8, 9 — see §3.1 table. (Gen 6:3 has bāśār without kāl; Gen 7:23 has no bāśār.)

claims.claim: NETS Gen 8:20–9:17 differs from MT in five unambiguous ways: 8:22 "summer and spring" (not "summer and winter"); 9:1 adds "and subdue it"; 9:6 "in return for this blood shall it be shed"; 8:21 paraphrases the yeṣer clause and renders "on account of mankind" as "because of the deeds of humans"; plus smaller renderings (9:2 "trembling", 9:11 "die by the water", 9:17 "I have made").
claims.evidence: NETS Genesis PDF (pp. 11–12) read in full, based on Wevers' Göttingen edition (1974). Limitation: two-column extraction interleaves text; verse boundaries reconstructed; the five differences are unambiguous.

claims.claim: The divine name shifts with the passage's movements: YHWH in 8:20–21, ʾĕ·lō·hîm from 9:1 on.
claims.evidence: Interlinear Gen 8–9 read directly.

claims.claim: BibleHub's own "Topical Lexicon" on the ʿānān (H6051) page is wrong on its own page: it claims "the word itself is not used in Genesis 9 for the rainbow covenant", while BDB sense 1b on the same page lists Gen 9:13, 14 (twice), 16, and the interlinear shows ʿānān in all three verses.
claims.evidence: BDB ʿānān sense 1b + interlinear Gen 9, read directly. (This is a finding about a source, not about the text; the Topical Lexicon is modern devotional commentary, NOT BDB.)

claims.claim: The purpose of Noah's sacrifice (8:20) is disputed among the commentators read: propitiation (Skinner; Ryle — "in an especial sense a propitiatory offering") vs. thanksgiving (Westermann following Cassuto; JFB — "first care… to return thanks"; Keil — thanksgiving for protection + prayer for future mercy). No consensus.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 157–158; Westermann pp. 451–452; JFB Gen 8; Keil Gen 8; Ryle pp. 114–115 — all read directly.

claims.claim: All commentators who discuss the "pleasing aroma" (8:21a) treat it as gracious acceptance, not a crude divine appetite.
claims.evidence: Skinner (refinement of Babylonian eudemonism); Keil (feelings of the offerer ascending in the vapour); Westermann (formalised sacrificial idiom; "he received favourably"); Ryle ("smell of complacence/satisfaction"); JFB ("acceptable as the most fragrant incense"); Clarke ("well pleased… in faith of the promised Savior") — all read directly.

claims.claim: The six commentators read are unanimous that 8:21b ("the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth") functions as the ground of divine restraint/mercy, not as a fresh indictment; they differ only in *how*.
claims.evidence: Skinner (appeal to clemency, since judgment cannot cure it); Keil (innate evil needs forbearance + Noah's offering as principal motive); Westermann ("era of patience" — God puts up with an unaltered human condition); JFB/Clarke (concessive "though/although"); Ryle (R.V. margin "for the" preferred for its emphasis on mercy) — all read directly.

claims.claim: Whether the rainbow was newly created at this point or a pre-existing phenomenon appointed as a sign is split: newly appeared (Skinner — "the most obvious assumption, though not perhaps inevitable"; Keil — "presupposes that it appeared then for the first time"); pre-existing and appointed (Westermann — "the rainbow, already there in the old narrative"; JFB — "set, that is, constitute or appoint"; Clarke — most explicit: "It cannot be rationally supposed that there was no rainbow in the heavens before the time mentioned in the text…"); Ryle genuinely two-sided, leaning new.
claims.evidence: Skinner p. 172; Keil Gen 9; Westermann pp. 472–473; JFB Gen 9; Clarke Gen 9; Ryle pp. 123–126 — all read directly.

claims.claim: The blood prohibition's rationale has six distinct formulations among the commentators read; the life-in-blood equation itself is established (clm-sc-011), but *why* the ban exists and how far it reaches is not agreed.
claims.evidence: Skinner (blood IS the life; life "must be restored to God before the flesh can be eaten"; the live-flesh/Abyssinian explanation is "a mistake"); Keil ("The soul of the animal is in the blood"; anti-cruelty + sacrifice as surrender of one's inmost life); Westermann (NOT a ban on blood as a substance — "one must pour out the life beforehand"; functional/pulsation understanding); JFB (narrow: only "to prevent these excesses of cannibal ferocity in eating flesh of living animals"); Clarke (typological/atonement — "the grand instrument of expiation… typical of that blood by which we enter into the holiest"; one of the seven Noahic precepts, renewed under the Christian dispensation, Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25); Ryle (blood "the vehicle of the soul, or vital principle (nephesh)… always offered in sacrifice to God as the most sacred part of the victim"). All read directly.

claims.claim: Whether the covenant includes the 9:1–7 ordinances or only the no-more-flood promise is an open question: Skinner presents both sides and leans inclusion as "probable" (analogy with the Abrahamic covenant); Westermann separates the covenant (promise only) from the blessing ordinances; Keil treats 9:1–7 as the covenant's "necessary complement" without posing the question.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 173–174, read directly (full quotation in §9); Westermann pp. 470–472, read directly; Keil Gen 9, read directly. JFB/Clarke/Ryle not verified in these terms (JFB's heading "Ge 9:1–7. Covenant" is a label, not an argument; Clarke has no note on 9:8–11).

claims.claim: The image-of-God basis for the 9:6 bloodshed law is explained four different ways: Keil (murder destroys the image; punishment belongs to divinely appointed rulers — "laid the foundation for all civil government"); Westermann (image = God's counterpart who "can have a history with God"; murder is "a direct attack on God's right of dominion"; 9:6 does NOT transfer God's authority to punish to humanity, against Delitzsch); JFB (image "injured by the fall, but… not lost"); Ryle (image = "man's higher nature, expressed by his self-consciousness, freedom of will, reason, affection, &c."). Skinner and Clarke are silent on it (Skinner cross-refers to 1:26 only).
claims.evidence: Keil Gen 9; Westermann pp. 464–469; JFB Gen 9; Ryle pp. 120–123 — all read directly. Skinner p. 170 ("On the image of God see on 1:26") and Clarke Gen 9 read directly.

claims.claim: Skinner holds that in P as in J the flood story closes with an assurance that is "absolute, not contingent on the behaviour of the creatures", and that the Noachic covenant is "the first of two covenants by which (according to this writer) the relations of the Almighty to His creatures are regulated".
claims.evidence: Skinner p. 171, read directly (covenant note, pp. 171–174 read in full).

claims.claim: Westermann holds that Gen 9:8–17 means God makes a promise, "not that he seals a covenant with them": berit here means "self-obligation, promise" (Kutsch, quoted by Westermann), and the extension to all animals proves "there can be no question of what is usually understood by covenant".
claims.evidence: Westermann pp. 469–472, read directly. (Kutsch is cited *through* Westermann; no separate Kutsch entry is proposed.)

claims.claim: The derivation of the rainbow symbol from the warrior's bow laid aside is disputed: Skinner derives it from thunderstorm imagery (Indra, Kuzah, Iris, the Edda bridge, Marduk's bow as a constellation) and says the flood connexion "would thus be a later, though still ancient, adaptation", noting "no Babylonian parallel has yet been discovered" for it; Westermann explicitly rejects the warrior-bow derivation for this passage as "very misleading".
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 172–173, read directly; Westermann pp. 472–473, read directly.

claims.claim: Keil defines the covenant as "the giving of a promise possessing the nature of a covenant" whose content is the no-flood assurance.
claims.evidence: Keil Gen 9, read directly (BibleHub "kad").

claims.claim: Source-critical assignments for the passage (Skinner: 8:20–22 J, 9:1–17 P; BDB sigla J/P as given) are scholarly positions, not established facts; no independent source-critical verification was done in this track.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 157–158, 169–174, read directly; BDB sigla quoted where BDB gives them.

claims.claim: In Atrahasis Tablet III the gods smell the fragrance and gather "like flies over the offering", and the divine response is population controls, not a covenant: no covenant language, no sign, no promise to humanity.
claims.evidence: Dalley, *Myths from Mesopotamia* (archive.org full text, L3728–L3740 and L3758–L3780, L3838–L3858), read directly. Offering itself largely lost in a lacuna ("gap of about 58 lines").

claims.claim: In Gilgamesh XI (Dalley) the gods smell the fragrance and "like flies gathered over the sacrifice", and the reward is individual immortality for Utnapishtim and his wife at the Mouth of the Rivers — no covenant, no sign, no promise to humanity.
claims.evidence: Dalley, same volume (L10256–L10274, L10276–L10288, L10364–L10390), read directly.

claims.claim: George's Gilgamesh XI reads "gathered like flies around the man making sacrifice" (XI 155–163), not "collected like flies over a sacrifice" as the background summary had it; Dalley's wording is closer to the background phrasing than George's, and the two translations must not be conflated.
claims.evidence: George via ETANA (citing Penguin 2000, pp. 88–99), XI 155–163 and 200–205, read directly.

claims.claim: In the Sumerian Flood Story, Ziusudra sacrifices oxen and innumerable sheep to Utu; An and Enlil grant him "life like a god" and settle him in Dilmun — no covenant with humanity, no sign.
claims.evidence: ETCSL t.1.7.4 — registry entry verified (full translation read 2026-11-16, Flood session); this session's re-check was an ETCSL search-result snippet only (direct open failed, not retried). The claim rests on the registry-verified full read, corroborated by the snippet.

claims.claim: Jubilees 6 is the closest parallel to Genesis 9 in this dossier: sacrifice, covenant, blood oath, bow-as-sign, and an annual renewal (Feast of Weeks) — all absent from the Mesopotamian flood stories.
claims.evidence: Jubilees 6:1–4, 6:10, 6:15–17 (Charles translation, 1913; earth-history.com), read directly. Chapter heading misprint "Gen. vii.20-2" for Gen. 8:20–22 noted.

claims.claim: Gen 9:8–17 lacks the Hittite suzerainty-treaty apparatus: no historical prologue, no document clause, no witness list of gods, no curses and blessings in treaty form; its parties are universal, not bilateral.
claims.evidence: Structural observation from the Gen 9 text itself (verified) against the six-element form as stated in Lucas, *Themelios* 8.1 (1982) — Lucas read directly in full 2026-11-17 (Themelios 8.1, September 1982: 19–23; biblicalstudies.org.uk full text): (1) Preamble, (2) Historical prologue, (3) Stipulations (basic, detailed), (4) Document clause (deposition of a copy and periodic reading), (5) Witnesses (a long list of gods), (6) Curses and blessings; Lucas also notes “Mendenhall’s thesis has never been without its critics, but opposition to it seems to be becoming increasingly fashionable.” Mendenhall’s and Korošec’s monographs were not opened. Assessment probable on that account.

claims.claim: In Enuma Elish Tablet VI, Marduk's bow is fixed as a Bow Star in heaven after his victory over Tiamat — not a rainbow in a cloud, not a covenant with humanity, not a weapon laid aside to signal peace. The ESV Study Bible note's "hangs his war bow in the clouds" phrasing is imprecise.
claims.evidence: King 1902 full text read directly 2026-11-17 (WikiChristian, Text:Enuma Elish): “They beheld the bow and how its work was accomplished... Then Anu raised the [...] in the assembly of the gods. He kissed the bow... And thus he named the names of the bow, saying, ‘Long-wood’ shall be one name, and the second name shall be [...], And its third name shall be the Bow-star, in heaven shall it [...]! Then he fixed a station for it...” The bow-naming passage stands at the end of Tablet V in King’s edition and in Tablet VI in Foster/Lambert’s edition; Foster was not opened in full, and Talon via search excerpt only. Assessment probable on that account.

claims.claim: The fly-necklace (Atrahasis/Gilgamesh XI) is a parallel *memorial-sign* motif — a visible token by which a deity remembers the flood — but it uses a necklace, not a bow/rainbow, and involves no covenant with humanity. It must not be presented as the rainbow's source.
claims.evidence: Dalley, Atrahasis L3776–L3780; Gilgamesh L10276–L10288; George XI 163–165 — read directly (§7.1).

claims.claim: The "bow laid aside" formulation is Skinner's (ICC, 1910, pp. 172–173), but it is not Skinner alone: it is taken up by Hastings' dictionary entry, Clines (1972), and in popular form by Luther and Kline (as reported). It is a scholarly interpretation of Hebrew *qeshet*, not a claim that Genesis borrows the Enuma Elish Bow Star.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 172–173 read directly by the commentaries track (superseding the ANE track’s “not opened directly” caveat, which was based on the Hastings quotation alone). Clines (Faith and Thought 100.2, 1972–3, pp. 128–142) read directly in full 2026-11-17 (gospelstudies.org.uk PDF): “the sign of the rainbow, God’s bow of war now laid aside”. Hastings’ Strahan “Rainbow” entry read directly in full 2026-11-17 (biblia.work reproduction of Hastings’ Dictionary of the Apostolic Church, signed James Strahan); it quotes Skinner, Genesis, p. 172 directly. Luther and Kline as reported in a 2026 sermon transcript (not cited as primary).

claims.claim: No verified link exists between Ishtar's bow and the rainbow in the sources consulted: the only source consulted (Talon) identifies the Bow Star with Ishtar's stellar incarnation, not with a rainbow.
claims.evidence: Talon via search-result excerpt; no primary-text passage on Ishtar's bow as a rainbow was opened. The question is unresolved, not answered.

claims.claim: Philo treats Gen. 8:20–9:17 in *Questions and Answers on Genesis*, Book II, §§50–64 — *not* Book III (Book III begins at Gen. 15:7).
claims.evidence: QG II, Yonge translation (earlyjewishwritings.com, book42.html, L1952–L2584), read directly 2026-11-17.

claims.claim: Philo (QG II.50) asks why Noah built an altar without being commanded, and answers that gratitude owed to God "ought to be offered to him without command, and without any delay or hesitation".
claims.evidence: QG II.50, read directly.

claims.claim: Philo (QG II.59) holds that the blood is "the substance of the soul" — "of that soul which exists by the external senses and by vitality, not of that which is spoken of with a certain especial pre-eminence, being the rational and intellectual soul".
claims.evidence: QG II.59, read directly.

claims.claim: Philo (QG II.62) holds that man was made "after the image of God" rather than after God's own image because "no mortal thing could have been formed on the similitude of the supreme Father of the universe, but only after the pattern of the second deity, who is the Word of the supreme Being".
claims.evidence: QG II.62, read directly.

claims.claim: Philo (QG II.64) holds that a bow is "not itself a weapon, but only an instrument for the use of weapons" — its arrow strikes at a distance while what is near remains unhurt — which is why it proves the whole earth will never again suffer a deluge.
claims.evidence: QG II.64, read directly.

claims.claim: Philo (QG II.63) reads "never again a deluge" as: various inundations may occur, but never one changing the whole earth into a lake or sea.
claims.evidence: QG II.63, read directly.

claims.claim: Josephus (Ant. 1.3.7–8) adds a motive Genesis does not state in that form: Noah's fear of annual flooding, and his prayer that nature go on in its "former orderly course"; God answers with the bow as a sign that He has "left off my anger".
claims.evidence: Josephus, *Antiquities* 1.3.7–8 (Whiston; godrules.net), read directly.

claims.claim: No treatment of the Noahic covenant or the rainbow as such was found in Augustine, *City of God* XV.26–27 or XVI.1–2; Augustine's post-flood comment there is typological (ark = Church; sons and vineyard = Christ / Church / heretics). The negative finding is limited to those chapters — no exhaustive search of the whole *City of God* was done.
claims.evidence: XV.26–27 (New Advent, Dods; L823–L911), read directly. XVI.1–2 via search-result excerpts only.

claims.claim: Chrysostom's Gen. 9 material is in Homily 27 (9:1–7) and Homily 28 (9:8–17), *not* Homily 26; Homily 26 covers Gen. 8:1–22.
claims.evidence: Hill translation, *Homilies on Genesis 18–45* — Homily 28 p. 187 read directly (FlipHTML5); Homily 27.13/27.15 via SermonIndex ECF excerpts; Homily 26's coverage established from the volume's contents as consulted.

claims.claim: Chrysostom (Hom. 28, p. 187) holds that the bow is given because of *human* limitations and fear, not because God needs to remember: "I will remember" is accommodated language "for us to fix our eyes on that sign given us and thus suspect no trouble".
claims.evidence: Homily 28, p. 187 (Hill, via FlipHTML5, L4–L18), read directly.

claims.claim: Chrysostom (Hom. 27.13) reads "flesh with its lifeblood" as "strangled" (an animal's blood is its soul), ties the reservation of blood to God to the sacrificial system, and sees the prohibition as a pre-emptive check on homicide; Hom. 27.15 renders 9:6 "his own will be shed in payment for that person's blood".
claims.evidence: Homily 27.13 and 27.15 via SermonIndex ECF excerpts only — *not a full-page open of the Hill volume*. Assessment probable on that account.

claims.claim: Rashi reads the covenant as a *confirmation and strengthening* of a promise already made in response to Noah's fear of propagating (9:9); the rainbow is the confirmation itself (9:11); the defective spelling of "generations" (9:12) marks generations so righteous they did not need the sign (Hezekiah's; R. Shimon bar Yochai's); and the sign works *forensically* — when the Standard of Justice accuses, God sees the sign (9:16).
claims.evidence: Rashi on Gen. 9:8–17 (Chabad), read directly 2026-11-17. No Rashi gloss was shown on 9:13 itself on that page.

claims.claim: Rashi (secondary only) reads "said in His heart" (8:21) as a resolution kept private and not revealed to Noah, and the doubled "I will not again" as an oath (Shevuos 36a) — the oath to which Isa 54:9 refers.
claims.evidence: Secondary only (janlemke.com citing Rashi; corroborated by Robert Alter's note, Sefaria Voices sheet 441639). Chabad/Sefaria for 8:21 not directly opened. Assessment probable on that account.

claims.claim: Targum Onkelos 9:6 adds a judicial procedure with no Hebrew counterpart — "by witnesses, upon the sentence of the judges, his blood shall be shed" — and renders the divine party in the covenant formulae as the Memra ("between My Word, and between you" / "between My Word and between the earth"); 9:13 retains "bow", not "rainbow".
claims.evidence: Targum Onkelos Gen. 9:1–17 (Etheridge translation, ebible.org), read directly.

claims.claim: The blood prohibition's rationale (life is in the blood) and the prohibition itself recur in Lev. 17:11 and Acts 15:20, 29; Leviticus adds an atonement function Genesis 9 does not state, and Acts re-imposes abstention from blood on Gentile believers. The relationship is a *thematic echo, not proven dependence* — no source opened establishes direct literary dependence.
claims.evidence: Lev. 17:11, Acts 15:20, 29 as given in BibleGateway *search-result excerpts (ESV/KJV), not a full-page open*. Assessment probable on that account.

claims.claim: Kessler holds the Noahic covenant is universal, unconditional, and God-only in its commitment — an unconditional, "pure promise of salvation from God for the whole world" (Zimmerli 1999:46) — and that its distinctiveness is the preservation of creation rather than the redemption of humankind.
claims.evidence: Kessler, "Jesus and the Jewish covenants," *Verbum et Ecclesia* (article 3794), read directly 2026-11-17. (Zimmerli cited through Kessler.)

claims.claim: The event has no independently established historical date (Standards §3.1); it is placed by narrative order (order 9) only, and no chronology is invented.
claims.evidence: Standards v1.1 §3.1 (methodological statement, not a historical finding).

claims.claim: The scope of "never again" is debated: the promise as worded is flood-specific (9:11, 15), but its extension beyond flood judgment is a live interpretive question (Philo: local inundations may occur; Josephus: extraordinary storms may come; Skinner: absolute promise; Westermann: basis of all life, shaken by no catastrophe).
claims.evidence: Gen 9:11, 15 wording (KJV + interlinear, read directly); Philo QG II.63, Josephus Ant. 1.3.8, Skinner p. 171, Westermann p. 472 — all read directly.

connections.note: The covenant first promised: “I will establish my covenant with thee” — the *identical* qûm form (wa·hă·qi·mō·ṯî) as 9:11. The 9:9–17 covenant is the fulfilment of the 6:18 promise. Established.
The blessing triad pĕrû ûrĕbû ûmilʾû repeated verbatim in 9:1 (and 9:7). Established.
The image of God — the stated ground of the 9:6 blood law (“for in the image of God made he man”). BDB ṣelem sense 2 cites Gen 1:26, 1:27, 9:6 together. Established.
The food gift: “as the green plant have I given you all things” (9:3) — same verb (nā·ṯ at·tî) and same “for food” phrase, verified directly. Established.
As the animals leave the ark they are told to swarm and “be fruitful, and multiply” — the same triad 9:7 echoes with šir·ṣū added. Established.
“The earth was filled with violence” / “the end of all flesh is come” — the judgment the covenant answers, and the “fill” (milʾû) now to be by life, not violence. Established.

The ground cursed (3:17); Lamech names Noah expecting comfort “concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed” (5:29); 8:21 lifts the curse on the ground (“I will not again curse the ground”). Thematic, not a quotation. Established as a thematic link.

The narrative continuation (Noah’s sons, the vineyard, Ham/Canaan) — the sibling event’s passage. Cited only as the continuation; its research belongs to the sibling track (Noah and His Sons). Cross-link both ways when both events are published. Established.

“For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth.” Quoted as the oath of the Gen 9:11 promise. *Overlap with conn-gf-03* (the Flood event claims it too) — the anchor here is the 9:11 oath specifically, not the flood; Rashi ties the oath to 8:21’s doubled promise (secondary source). Cross-link both ways; do not present as two different connections. Established.

“If ye can break my covenant of the day, and my covenant of the night…” — the covenant with day and night, answering 8:22’s day/night ordinance; BDB bĕrît II.2.a cites Jer 33:20, 25 with Gen 9:9–17. Established.

“As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about.” BDB qešet sense 2 cites Ezek 1:28 for comparison with Gen 9:13, 14, 16. Thematic. Established.
“And there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.” The bow-sign carried into the throne vision. Thematic. Established.

“For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make an atonement for your souls.” Same rationale as Gen 9:4, with an atonement function Genesis does not state. *Thematic echo, not proven dependence.* Probable (wording via BibleGateway search excerpts, not a full-page open).

“Abstain from… things strangled, and from blood.” The blood abstention re-imposed on Gentile believers. *Thematic echo, not proven dependence.* Probable (wording via BibleGateway search excerpts, not a full-page open).

review.notes: Content phase (branch: content/noah-sacrifice-covenant). Stage 1 research dossier 2026-11-16/17 (workspace: gnosis-sacrifice-covenant/dossier/noahs-sacrifice-and-covenant-research-dossier.md), base main b3b89ac. Claims register: 67 of the dossier's 68 claims (clm-sc-001–068 except clm-sc-046, held out — see D6 below); assessments established 52, probable 6, debated 8, unknown 1. Connections: 14 (conn-sc-01–14); the 5 rejected connections (Heb 11:7, 1 Pet 3:20–21, Matt 24:37–39, 2 Pet 2:5, 3:5–6) are not added. Sources: 27 (20 reused registry entries, all verified on main, plus 7 new verified entries: Kessler, Mastnjak, Finlay, Clines, Lucas, Hastings, Enuma Elish). EM decisions applied (2026-11-16): D3 — Gen 9:6 rendering PENDING Yonatan's decision; clm-sc-014 stays debated with both readings in evidence (traditional agent/instrument “by man” vs Mastnjak's bĕth pretii “for [the] man”, NETS adopts pretii; no textual variant); the prose uses the traditional rendering with a dispute note as PROVISIONAL text, clearly marked pending D3. D6 — the 9 not-independently-verified new sources were verified directly where a claim needed them: Lucas (Themelios 8.1, 1982: 19–23, full text), Clines (Faith and Thought 100.2, 1972–3, pp. 128–142, full PDF), Hastings' Strahan “Rainbow” entry (Dictionary of the Apostolic Church reproduction, full text), and Enuma Elish (King 1902 full text; bow-naming passage at the end of Tablet V in King's edition, Tablet VI in Foster/Lambert's edition) are added as verified and cited; Weinfeld (JAOS 90.2, 1970, full PDF), Muswubi (Verbum et Ecclesia 45(1), 2024, full text), and Majesty (Asian Journal of Natural Sciences 4.3, 2025, full PDF) were also read directly but are NOT added, because no included claim cites them (Weinfeld and Muswubi support only the held-out clm-sc-046; Majesty supports no claim). Freedman could not be verified directly (the Marín García Scribd copy of “Covenant and circumcision in Gen. 17” was not accessible in two searches), and Bible Odyssey was not opened in full and supports no claim; neither is added. HELD OUT: clm-sc-046 (grant/unilateral reading, probable) — its claim as written names Freedman among the holders, and Freedman remains unverified; the claim is held out of the event JSON rather than restated, for the EM to decide (e.g. include without Freedman, or verify Freedman another way). No claim cites BibleHub's Topical Lexicon on ʿānān (clm-sc-027 records its error as a source finding). D5 — registry scope appends for the 20 reused entries (Gen 8:20–9:17 ranges, dossier §13.1) ride in a SEPARATE follow-up PR, not this one; no existing registry entry was edited here. D1 — conn-sc-09 (Isa 54:9, 9:11-oath anchor) is kept alongside the Flood's conn-gf-03, cross-linked; the conn-sc-09 note states the overlap explicitly. D4 — “never again” stays flood-specific (9:11, 15); Philo/Josephus local-flood readings are reception, not the text's claim. D2 — Wenham/Hamilton unread; no positions attributed. Corrections carried in: Philo QG Book II §§50–64 (not Book III); Chrysostom Homilies 27–28 (not 26); George “gathered like flies around the man making sacrifice”; Enuma Elish bow fixed as a star, not hung in clouds. Note: the dossier proposed the Hastings entry as Hastings' Dictionary of the New Testament; the text read is the Dictionary of the Apostolic Church entry (signed James Strahan), so the registry entry is recorded under that dictionary. No editorialOverride. Status in-review; publication is a separate decision and is NOT part of this PR.
